# Welcome to Invoke Toolkit documentation


<img alt="PyPI - Package Version" src="https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/invoke-toolkit">

::: {.callout-warning}
This software is in early development. Expect API breakages until version `0.1.x` is
released.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
`invoke-toolkit` extends [`invoke`](https://docs.pyinvoke.org/en/stable/) classes and functions prepending `ToolkitXXX`
for each extended class.

For compatiblity, when you do `from invoke_toolkit import task, Context` the names are preserved.
:::

Invoke Toolkit is a set of opinionated extensions to the popular [Python invoke library](https://pyinvoke.org)
that allow to create easy to use automation focuses scripts, with the ability to share them in different ways (packages, repos, etc).

It takes advantage of some recent developments in the Python ecosystem such as [`inline scripting`](https://peps.python.org/pep-0723/),
the [`rich`](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/introduction.html) and [`uv`](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv) pacakge manager.


Among its core features it extends the `Context` class with status updates

* <details>
  <summary>
  Add's some `Context` attributes such as `ctx.status()` or `ctx.print` using [rich](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/introduction.html)
  </summary>

    ```{.python}
    @task()
    def long_task(ctx: Context):
        with ctx.status("Doing something slow"):
            ctx.run("sleep 1")
    ```
</details>

* Renames the `inv`/`invoke` to `it`/`invoke-toolkit`, reads the same `tasks.py`.
* Replaces `print()` with `rich`'s Console print (internal logging uses `rich` logger): `it -d`.
* Command echo defaults to `stderr` (`it -e`)
* <details>
  <summary>
  Populates with built in collections to manage *plugins*
  </summary>
  ```bash
  it -xl
  ```
  </details>


## Installation

The recommended way to use `invoke-toolkit` is through `uv` package manager:

```bash
uv tool install invoke-toolkit
```

### Ad-hoc run with `uvx`/`pipx`

With `uvx` or `uv tool run`
```bash
uvx invoke-toolkit
```

With `pipx`
```bash
pipx run invoke-toolkit
```

## Managing uv tool plugins

When invoke-toolkit is installed persistently with [`uv tool
install`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/tools/), plugin distributions must
be installed into that same isolated environment. A plugin is identified by an
`invoke_toolkit.collection` entry point, not by an `invoke-toolkit-` package-name
prefix.

```console
intk -x plugin.list
intk -x plugin.add 'invoke-toolkit-example>=1'
intk -x plugin.add git+https://github.com/example/invoke-toolkit-example.git
intk -x plugin.add ./invoke-toolkit-example
intk -x plugin.link ./invoke-toolkit-example
intk -x plugin.update --name invoke-toolkit-example
intk -x plugin.update
intk -x plugin.remove invoke-toolkit-example
```

`plugin.add` maps to uv's `--with` option and accepts registry requirements,
Git or archive URLs, and local paths. A local path is built into a static
installation. `plugin.link` maps to `--with-editable`; edits in that checkout
are immediately visible.

`plugin.update NAME` refreshes and reinstalls one non-editable plugin. Without
a name, it refreshes every directly installed non-editable plugin and reports
editable plugins as skipped. Registry version constraints and pinned Git
references are preserved. Static local plugins are rebuilt from their current
contents. Plugin updates never update the base invoke-toolkit requirement.

Shell completion suggests directly installed plugin distribution names for
`plugin.remove` and named `plugin.update` operations.

Every mutation reconstructs `uv tool install` from the active tool's receipt,
preserving unrelated supplemental requirements. Commands fail rather than
guess when run through `uvx`, `uv run`, a project environment, or an
installation managed by another package manager.

### pipx equivalent

pipx can inject and remove packages in the invoke-toolkit environment manually:

```console
pipx inject invoke-toolkit PLUGIN
pipx inject invoke-toolkit --editable ./PLUGIN
pipx uninject invoke-toolkit PLUGIN
pipx list --include-injected
```

`PLUGIN` may be a registry, local, or Git source accepted by pip. See the
[`pipx inject` documentation](https://pipx.pypa.io/latest/how-to/inject-packages.html).
invoke-toolkit does not detect or execute pipx lifecycle operations, and does
not claim exact update parity with uv.

### Isolated maintainer verification

The lifecycle smoke test installs the current checkout and two fixture plugins
inside `ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:trixie`:

```console
uv run invoke uv-plugin-integration
```

It requires Docker, Podman, or another runtime recognized by
`find-container-tool`. It is intentionally outside the default nox matrix.


## Simple task example

```python
from invoke_toolkit import task, Context

@task()
def build(ctx: Context):
    ctx.run("quarto build")
```

## Async tasks and commands

Task functions declared with `async def` are supported automatically:

```{.python}
import asyncio
from invoke_toolkit import Context, task

@task
async def build(ctx: Context):
    result = await ctx.run("quarto build", hide=True)
    await ctx.run_async("printf done")
    return result
```

Inside an async task, `ctx.run()` is awaitable and uses the native asyncio
subprocess path. `ctx.run_async()` is the explicit coroutine API. Synchronous
tasks keep Invoke's normal blocking `ctx.run()` behavior, including its
`asynchronous=True` Promise API.

Use `ctx.gather()` when a task needs explicit concurrent command or coroutine
work. Submitted work starts immediately; `gather.results` is ordered by
submission:

```{.python}
@task
async def parallel(ctx: Context):
    async with ctx.gather() as gather:
        gather(ctx.run_async("first", hide=True))
        gather(ctx.run_async("second", hide=True))
    return gather.results
```

Async task execution remains sequential by default. Async execution supports
configured shell, environment, command prefixes, output hiding/streaming,
`warn`, `dry`, timeout, and cancellation cleanup. Native async commands reject
PTY mode, interactive stdin, and Invoke stream watchers; use synchronous
`ctx.run()` for those features. Task argument parsing, aliases, help, shell
completion callbacks, and file completion markers remain available for async
tasks.
